title: Arm's Length: Price Every Deal With Yourself as if You Were Strangers
summary: When two companies you own trade with each other, the price decides which country taxes the profit. Transfer pricing rules require that price to be what unrelated parties would have agreed. This lesson teaches the principle, the main methods, and how a developer's ordinary fees fall inside it.
body:
The moment two companies you control pay each other for anything, a fee, a loan, a service or a licence, you have set a price that moves profit between them, and every tax authority involved has the right to ask whether strangers would have agreed the same price.

Recall

Q. Name the four families of interest-limitation rules.

A. Ratio tests, earnings tests, arm's-length tests and recharacterisation.

Q. Why do many systems treat passive income of a foreign affiliate differently from active business income?

A. Because passive income, such as interest or rent with no real business behind it, is easy to park offshore, so many systems tax it at home as it arises rather than when it is paid home. Verify the rules against the primary source.

Q. What are OSHA's Focus Four hazards in construction?

A. Falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer with a holding company and project companies in more than one country charges fees between them almost by reflex: a development management fee, a share of head-office costs, interest on a shareholder loan, a fee for a guarantee the parent gives the bank. Each of those is a price. If the paying company is in one country and the receiving company in another, the price decides where profit is taxed. Transfer pricing is the body of rules that tests those prices. I teach it this week because it is one of the most common points on which a tax authority challenges a cross-border structure, and because the defence is almost entirely evidence made at the time.

The arm's-length principle

Plain English. Pretend the two companies are strangers who each want the best deal. What price would they have agreed? That is the arm's-length price. If your actual price differs, the tax authority may adjust your taxable profit to what it would have been at the arm's-length price.

The professional framing comes from international guidance, most widely the transfer pricing guidelines published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which many countries follow or draw on in their own laws. The guidance asks two things. First, what was actually done: the functions each company performed, the assets it used and the risks it really carried. This is called a functional analysis. Second, what unrelated parties doing comparable things in comparable circumstances charged. Those reference points are called comparables. How far any country's law follows that guidance must be verified against the primary source.

The test is not "was the price reasonable". It is "would strangers in this position, doing these things, with these risks, have agreed this price". A fee can look modest and still fail if the receiving company did almost nothing to earn it.

Say that out loud now.

The main methods

There are five classic methods, and you need only know what each is for. The comparable uncontrolled price method compares your price directly with the price in a similar deal between unrelated parties, and is best when an almost identical outside deal exists, such as a loan or a commodity. The resale price method starts from the price at which a distributor resells and works back to a margin. The cost plus method takes the supplier's costs and adds a mark-up that comparable independent suppliers earn, and suits routine services. The transactional net margin method compares a company's profit margin on the activity with the margins of comparable independent companies. The profit split method divides combined profit between related parties according to what each contributed, used where both make unique contributions.

For a developer, three of these do most of the work: comparable uncontrolled price for interest and guarantee fees, cost plus for shared services, and a comparison with fees charged by independent development managers for development management.

Worked example one: a development management fee

A hypothetical parent company provides development management to a project company in another country: securing approvals, managing consultants and the contractor, reporting to the lender. Hard construction cost is 20,000,000 dollars. The parent charges a fee of 6 percent of hard cost, 1,200,000 dollars, deducted by the project company.

The arm's-length question has three parts. What did the parent actually do? If its staff ran the project day to day, signed consultant appointments and carried the management workload, it performed the functions. If a local team in the project company did all of that and the parent only attended two board meetings, the parent did very little. What do independent development managers charge for comparable work? Suppose, hypothetically, that published or quoted fees for comparable projects run from 3 to 5 percent of hard cost. And is there overlap? If the project company also pays a local manager for the same work, the parent's fee may be duplicated.

In this hypothetical, a 6 percent fee sits above the comparable range. If the authority adjusts the fee to 4 percent, 800,000 dollars, it denies 400,000 dollars of deduction in the project company. The parent may already have paid tax on the full 1,200,000 dollars in its own country, so 400,000 dollars is now taxed twice unless relief is obtained. Day 4 covers that relief.

Worked example two: shared head-office costs

The parent's head office spends 300,000 dollars a year on accounting, legal coordination and reporting, serving four project companies equally. Using cost plus with a hypothetical arm's-length mark-up of 5 percent, total charge is 315,000 dollars, and each project company bears 78,750 dollars. The allocation key, equal shares, must be justified: if one project takes most of the effort, an allocation by time or by assets is more defensible. And the services must actually be received. A charge for "stewardship", meaning the parent watching its own investment, is usually not a service to the subsidiary at all and is often disallowed.

How the best do it

Disciplined multinational groups set their intercompany prices in a written policy at the start of the year, with a benchmark study supporting each type of charge, intercompany agreements signed before services begin, and invoices that match the agreements. They test actual results against the policy at year end and correct before the books close, not after an audit. A small developer can copy this with one page per charge type: what is provided, by whom, the method, the comparable range and the agreement it rests on.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: every intercompany price is a potential adjustment in two countries; verify each country's rules against the primary source. Liability: intercompany service agreements create real obligations between your companies, including to perform. Banking: lenders cap or subordinate related-party fees and will ask how each is set. Governance: both boards approve each intercompany agreement and its pricing method. Estate: recurring intercompany fees decide where wealth accumulates in the group, which your succession plan must reflect. Exit: a buyer will strip out fees above arm's length when it values the project, and will ask for indemnities against past adjustments.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each country, with transfer pricing experience; for material charges, a benchmark study prepared by a specialist.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is setting intercompany prices by what you want each company to earn, then hoping no one asks. The control is a written transfer pricing policy, set before the year begins, supported by comparables and signed agreements.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that because he owns both companies, the fee between them is his business alone. It is the business of both tax authorities.

Callback

In Week 56, Elias and Ford taught residence and substance: a company is where its mind and management really sit, and a substance record proves it. Transfer pricing applies the same idea to income. A fee belongs to the company that actually performed the work, and the functional analysis is the substance record for each charge.

Recap

Every price between related companies must be the price strangers would agree. Find out what each company really did, find comparables, choose the right method, and document it before the year starts. A fee above the range is adjusted, and the adjustment can tax the same profit twice.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: GlaxoSmithKline in the Supreme Court of Canada, 2012.
checklist: I have listed every payment between my own companies, including fees, interest and guarantees.
Each charge has a written agreement signed before the service began.
I know which company actually performed the functions and carried the risks.
Each charge has a pricing method and a comparable range on file.
I have checked shared-cost allocation keys against actual effort.
I do not charge subsidiaries for the parent's own stewardship.
Both boards have approved each intercompany agreement.
A tax adviser with transfer pricing experience has reviewed the policy in each country.
head: Field checklist
speak: Whenever two of my companies pay each other, for a development fee, shared costs, a loan or a guarantee, I have set a price that moves profit between countries. Transfer pricing rules require that price to be the one strangers would have agreed. The test has two parts. First, what did each company really do, what assets did it use and what risks did it carry. Second, what did unrelated parties charge for comparable work. The common methods for a developer are a direct comparable price for loans and guarantees, cost plus a market mark-up for shared services, and comparison with independent development managers' fees. If my fee is above the range, the authority adjusts it, and the same profit can be taxed in both countries. So I write a pricing policy before the year begins, sign agreements before services start, and keep the comparables on file.
terms: Arm's-length principle — the rule that prices between related parties should match what unrelated parties would agree in comparable circumstances.
Functional analysis — a description of the functions each party performs, the assets it uses and the risks it actually bears in a transaction.
Comparables — transactions or companies between unrelated parties similar enough to serve as a reference for an arm's-length price.

hostile.q: Your project company paid its parent a 6 percent development fee. Independent managers charge less. Why shouldn't I reduce it?
hostile.a: You may be right, and I would rather show you the evidence than argue the number. Here is the intercompany agreement signed before work began, the functional analysis showing which parent staff did which work, and the benchmark of independent fees. If the benchmark range is below 6 percent, I accept an adjustment to the range, and I will ask our adviser to seek relief in the parent's country so the difference is not taxed twice.

title: GlaxoSmithKline, 2012: A Price Tested Without Its Bundle
summary: In 2012 the Supreme Court of Canada decided a transfer pricing dispute over what a Canadian pharmaceutical company paid a related foreign supplier for an ingredient. The case ran for many years, and both sides' early framing failed in some way. Seven steps, ending in Rule 61.
body:
A Canadian company paid a related supplier far more for an ingredient than generic buyers paid for the same chemical, and the dispute lasted many years because the price could not be judged without the licence it travelled with.

Recall

Q. What does a functional analysis describe?

A. The functions each party performs, the assets it uses and the risks it actually bears in a transaction.

Q. What is Rule 60?

A. Never move money between your own companies until a signed agreement and board approvals in both companies say what it is, on terms a stranger would accept; and never date a document earlier than the day it was signed.

Q. What is the multi-employer doctrine on a construction site?

A. The principle, in United States workplace safety enforcement, that more than one employer on a site, such as a general contractor that controls the site, can be cited for a hazard even if its own workers were not the ones exposed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is the leading transfer pricing case in Canada, and it is useful precisely because it is not about fraud. It is about how a price between related companies is tested, and what happens when the evidence was not built for that test. I describe the case at the level of principle. Verify every detail against the published judgments before you cite them; I give no figures because you should take them from the source.

1. Timeline

In the early 1990s, Glaxo Canada, the Canadian subsidiary of the Glaxo group, bought ranitidine, the active ingredient in its branded ulcer medicine Zantac, from a related company in Switzerland. Generic drug makers in Canada were buying ranitidine from unrelated suppliers at a far lower price. The Canadian tax authority reassessed Glaxo Canada for several tax years in that period, taking the view that the price it paid its affiliate exceeded a reasonable arm's-length price, using the generic purchase prices as the comparable. The Tax Court of Canada largely upheld the reassessment in 2008. The Federal Court of Appeal allowed Glaxo's appeal in 2010 and sent the matter back. The Supreme Court of Canada, in 2012, agreed that the matter should go back to the Tax Court, holding that the price had to be assessed in light of all the circumstances an arm's-length purchaser would consider, including a separate licence agreement under which Glaxo Canada obtained rights such as the use of the trademark and access to the group's products.

2. Key decisions

On the group's side, the key decision was to bundle the right to sell a branded product, its trademark and its support into an arrangement where a large part of the value was paid through the price of the ingredient, under a supply agreement separate from the licence. On the tax authority's side, the key decision was to test the ingredient price alone, against generic buyers who received a chemical and nothing else.

3. Assumptions

The group appears to have assumed that a price consistent with the group's commercial arrangements would be accepted. The authority assumed that ranitidine is ranitidine, so the generic price was the best comparable. The Supreme Court's answer, in substance, was that a buyer in Glaxo Canada's position would not have been buying only a chemical, so a comparable that bought only a chemical was not truly comparable.

4. Incentives

A multinational has an incentive to locate profit where it is taxed less, and the price of goods between affiliates is one way profit moves. The tax authority has an incentive to protect its tax base, and the cleanest available comparable is tempting. Neither incentive is improper. Both bias the analysis in a predictable direction, which is why the evidence must be built to survive the other side's bias.

5. Warning signs ignored

The warning sign anyone could see was the size of the gap between the related-party price and the open-market price for the same ingredient. A gap that large does not prove the price wrong, but it guarantees a challenge, and it demands a contemporaneous explanation of exactly what the extra price was paying for. A second warning sign was that the value of the brand and licence was delivered through one contract and paid for through another, which makes the price of each harder to defend separately.

Say that out loud now.

6. Point of no return

For the taxpayer, the point of no return was the end of each tax year without a documented analysis linking the ingredient price to the bundle of rights it purchased. After that, the explanation had to be reconstructed in litigation, years later, through expert evidence rather than records. For the authority, the point of no return was building the reassessment on a comparable that left out the licence, which the courts eventually found was the wrong frame. The result, for both, was a dispute that stretched over many years before the highest court sent it back for reconsideration.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a price separated from the bundle it paid for. When related parties split one commercial bargain across several contracts, each contract's price stops meaning anything on its own, and a tax authority will test the one it can most easily compare. The defence is to analyse and document the whole bundle, at the time, and to choose comparables that buy the same bundle.

What Cole would have asked in year one

Four questions, asked before the first invoice, would have changed the shape of this dispute. What exactly does the Canadian company receive for each dollar it pays, item by item? Which of those items could it buy from a stranger, and at what price? If it could not buy the brand and the licence from a stranger, what would a licensee in its position typically pay for them, and how? And does the combined price leave the Canadian company with a return that an independent distributor doing the same work would accept? Answered on paper in the first year, those questions become the evidence. Answered for the first time in a courtroom, they become an expert's opinion against another expert's.

What this means for a developer

You will never buy ranitidine, but you will bundle. A parent company may provide a project company with development management, a brand, a guarantee to the bank and access to its contractor relationships, and charge one fee, or several fees under several agreements. Test the whole package. Write down what each part is worth and why. If the development fee looks high, the reason may be that it also pays for the parent's guarantee; then say so in the agreement and in the analysis, or charge a separate guarantee fee priced on its own comparables. Never let the explanation exist only in your head.

Rule 61

Rule 61: Never set an intercompany price without a written analysis, made at the time, of the whole bundle the payment buys, tested against comparables that buy the same bundle.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is splitting one bargain across several intercompany contracts and pricing each by convenience. The control is a single annual transfer pricing memo for each project company that lists every intercompany agreement together, describes the combined bundle, and shows the pricing of each part.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads this case as a win for the taxpayer. It is better read as a warning: a dispute that lasted many years and was sent back for reconsideration is a cost in itself, whoever eventually prevails.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught that substance outweighs form. Here substance worked in both directions: the authority could not ignore the licence because it was a separate contract, and the taxpayer could not rely on the supply contract's price without explaining the substance of what it bought. Substance over form is not a weapon for one side; it is the rule both are judged by.

Recap

Glaxo Canada paid a related supplier much more than generic buyers paid for the same ingredient. The authority compared the ingredient alone; the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012 held that the licence and other circumstances had to be considered, and sent the case back. Rule 61 demands a contemporaneous analysis of the whole bundle.

Next: Sage on The Money: how intercompany fees move project cost, yield on cost and the investor's return.
checklist: I list every intercompany agreement for a project company together, not one by one.
I can describe the whole bundle each project company receives from the group.
Each part of the bundle has its own price and method, or the combined fee says what it covers.
Large gaps between my price and open-market prices have a written explanation.
Comparables buy the same bundle, not just one component.
The pricing memo is written each year, before the books close.
I verify any case detail against the published judgment before relying on it.
A transfer pricing specialist reviews material bundles.
head: Field checklist
speak: In the early 1990s, Glaxo Canada bought the active ingredient of its branded ulcer drug from a related Swiss company at a price far above what generic makers paid unrelated suppliers. The tax authority reassessed, using the generic prices as the comparable. After the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal, the Supreme Court of Canada held in 2012 that the price had to be judged in light of everything an arm's-length buyer would consider, including a separate licence giving rights to the brand, and sent the case back. The root cause was a price separated from the bundle it paid for. For a developer, that bundle might be development management, a brand, a guarantee and relationships. Rule 61: never set an intercompany price without a written analysis, made at the time, of the whole bundle the payment buys, tested against comparables that buy the same bundle.
terms: Bundle — a group of goods, services and rights supplied together, whose value may be paid for through one price or several.
Comparable uncontrolled price — the price charged in a comparable transaction between unrelated parties.
Reassessment — a tax authority's revision of a filed tax return, usually increasing tax owed.

hostile.q: Your project company pays the parent a development fee well above what independent managers charge. What else is it paying for?
hostile.a: It also covers the parent's completion guarantee to the senior lender and the parent's staff time on procurement. Our annual pricing memo lists all three elements, prices the guarantee separately against guarantee fee comparables and the management element against independent manager fees, and reconciles the total to the fee in the agreement. Here is the memo for this year, written before the books closed.

rule: Rule 61: Never set an intercompany price without a written analysis, made at the time, of the whole bundle the payment buys, tested against comparables that buy the same bundle.

title: What an Intercompany Fee Does to Cost, Value and Return
summary: An intercompany fee is not money moved from one pocket to another. It raises project cost, can lower net operating income and value, changes what outside investors earn, and, if it is adjusted, can be taxed twice. This lesson prices each effect with hypothetical round numbers.
body:
A fee your parent charges your project company looks like money moved between your own pockets, but it changes the project's cost, its value and its outside investors' return, and an adjustment can make the same dollar taxable twice.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the GlaxoSmithKline case, as Ford framed it?

A. A price separated from the bundle it paid for: the ingredient price was tested without the licence and other rights it travelled with.

Q. What is a return of capital, and why is it often treated differently from a dividend?

A. A repayment of the shareholder's own invested capital rather than a distribution of profit. Many systems do not tax it as income, though it usually needs formal company-law steps. Verify against the primary source.

Q. What is a job hazard analysis?

A. A step-by-step review of a task that identifies the hazard at each step and the control that will be used, done before the work starts.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when you own every company in the chain, an intercompany fee feels free. When anyone else is involved, a lender, a joint venture partner, an outside investor or a future buyer, it is not. Each of them sees the fee as a cost of the project paid to the sponsor, and each will ask whether it is at market. Every figure here is a hypothetical round number.

Effect one: cost and yield on cost

Yield on cost is stabilised net operating income (NOI) divided by total development cost. It is the developer's first test of whether a project creates value.

A hypothetical project has total development cost of 30,000,000 dollars and stabilised NOI of 2,100,000 dollars. Yield on cost is 2,100,000 divided by 30,000,000, which is 7.0 percent.

The parent now charges a development management fee of 1,200,000 dollars, capitalised into the cost of the building. Total cost becomes 31,200,000 dollars. Yield on cost becomes 2,100,000 divided by 31,200,000, which is about 6.73 percent. If the market cap rate for the finished building is 5.5 percent, the development spread, yield on cost minus cap rate, falls from 1.5 percentage points to about 1.23. In a joint venture where the partner's equity funds part of that fee, the partner is paying the sponsor 1,200,000 dollars and will want to know exactly what for.

Effect two: NOI and value

Now suppose that after stabilisation the parent also charges an asset management fee of 2 percent of gross revenue. Gross revenue is 3,000,000 dollars, so the fee is 60,000 dollars a year. If it sits above the NOI line, NOI falls to 2,040,000 dollars.

At a 5.5 percent cap rate, value is NOI divided by the cap rate. Before the fee, 2,100,000 divided by 0.055 is about 38,180,000 dollars. After it, 2,040,000 divided by 0.055 is about 37,090,000 dollars. A 60,000 dollar annual fee costs roughly 1,090,000 dollars of value on paper. In practice, a buyer or appraiser will usually remove a related-party fee and substitute a market-rate management cost, so the true question is whether your fee is above market. If it is, the excess is the part a buyer will refuse to pay for.

Say that out loud now.

Effect three: the outside investor's return

Suppose an outside investor holds 50 percent of the project company's equity. Every dollar of intercompany fee paid to the parent is a dollar that would otherwise have been profit shared half and half. A fee of 1,200,000 dollars therefore transfers 600,000 dollars from the investor to the sponsor, before tax. That is why joint venture agreements cap related-party fees, require them to be at market, and often require the investor's consent to any new one. JAX taught alignment in the waterfall in Week 38; intercompany fees are the quiet way that alignment breaks.

Effect four: the cost of an adjustment

Return to Day 1's hypothetical. The tax authority in the project's country reduces the development fee by 400,000 dollars to bring it within the comparable range. Using hypothetical rates taken from no country, a 30 percent project-country rate and a 25 percent parent-country rate: the project company loses a deduction worth 120,000 dollars. The parent has already paid 100,000 dollars of tax on that same 400,000 dollars of fee income. Unless the parent's country gives a matching reduction, total tax on that 400,000 dollars is 220,000 dollars, a 55 percent rate, plus interest and possibly a penalty. Relief mechanisms exist, which Day 4 covers, but they are slow and not guaranteed. Verify every rate and relief rule against the primary source.

Effect five: the project-level IRR

An intercompany fee does not change the combined return of the sponsor across both companies if you own everything, ignoring tax. But your internal rate of return (IRR) on the project company, the number a lender or investor looks at, falls, because the fee is a cost to the project and income to the parent. Always present two numbers: the project return after all intercompany fees at market, and the sponsor's total return including fees, and never mix them.

Effect six: the senior lender's view

A senior construction lender reads every related-party fee as money leaving the project for the sponsor while its loan is at risk. Practice varies and is commercial, not a standard, but three patterns are common. The lender may cap the development fee as a percentage of cost, often at a level it regards as market. It may require part of the fee to be deferred, paid only from cash after completion or after the in-balance test is passed, so that the sponsor's own fee is the first money at risk if the budget runs over. And after stabilisation it will usually underwrite any asset or property management fee as an operating cost at a market rate, whatever you actually charge, and subordinate any excess to debt service.

Worked through: if 600,000 dollars of the 1,200,000 dollar fee is deferred and the project overruns by 600,000 dollars, the deferred fee absorbs the overrun and is never paid. Your transfer pricing file still says 1,200,000 dollars was the arm's-length price. That is consistent, provided the agreement itself says the deferred part is contingent on completion within budget; then the contingency is part of the bargain, and comparables should be chosen with the same feature.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's view for your personal balance sheet: fees reach the parent early and in cash, which helps liquidity, while profit in the project company is paid late and depends on the exit. But fees are usually taxed as ordinary income in the year earned, while value held in the project may be taxed differently and later. Treat intercompany fees as compensation for real work, priced at market, not as a way to pull value forward. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal tax or investment decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting a project return to lenders and partners that quietly includes or excludes your own fees. The control is a two-column return summary, project return and sponsor return, with every intercompany fee listed and benchmarked.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a high intercompany fee "costs nothing because it is all mine". It costs yield on cost, value at exit, partner trust and, if adjusted, tax twice.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught net operating income, cap rates and the development spread. Every one of those numbers moves when an intercompany fee is added. The development spread is the margin for error, and a related-party fee above market spends that margin before the first tenant arrives.

Recap

An intercompany fee raises cost and lowers yield on cost, can lower NOI and value, transfers return from outside investors to the sponsor, and, if adjusted, can tax the same dollar twice. Price fees at market and show project and sponsor returns separately.

Next: Elias on The Rules: documentation, adjustments, relief from double tax, and Two Systems.
checklist: I list every intercompany fee in the pro forma, capitalised or above the NOI line.
I know what each fee does to yield on cost and the development spread.
I know whether a buyer would strip each fee out and substitute a market cost.
My joint venture agreement caps related-party fees and requires them at market.
I present project return and sponsor return separately.
I have priced the cost of an adjustment, including double tax.
I treat fees as pay for real work, not as a way to pull value forward.
A licensed adviser has reviewed the personal tax effect of fee income.
head: Field checklist
speak: An intercompany fee is not free just because I own both companies. Take a hypothetical 30 million dollar project with 2.1 million of NOI: a seven percent yield on cost. Add a 1.2 million dollar development fee from my parent and yield on cost drops to about 6.7 percent, eating into my margin over the cap rate. A 60,000 dollar annual asset management fee above the NOI line costs about a million dollars of value at a 5.5 percent cap rate, although a buyer will usually replace it with a market cost and refuse to pay for any excess. With a 50 percent outside investor, every fee moves half its value from them to me, which is why joint venture agreements cap fees. And if a tax authority cuts my fee, the same income can be taxed in both countries. So I price fees at market and show project and sponsor returns separately.
terms: Yield on cost — stabilised net operating income divided by total development cost.
Development spread — yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the developer's margin for creating value.
Double taxation — the same income taxed in two countries, often after one country adjusts a transfer price and the other does not.

hostile.q: Your pro forma shows a 7 percent yield on cost. Does that include the fees your own company charges the project?
hostile.a: It does not, and you are right to ask. With our 1,200,000 dollar development fee capitalised, yield on cost is about 6.73 percent, and that is the number we should both underwrite. Here is the list of every related-party fee, the agreement for each, the benchmark showing it sits within the market range, and our two-column summary of project return and sponsor return.

title: Documentation, Adjustments and Relief: How Transfer Pricing Is Enforced
summary: Transfer pricing is enforced through documentation, adjustments, penalties and, if you are lucky, relief from double tax. This lesson teaches the life cycle of a transfer pricing challenge as concepts, and compares in principle how Canada and Guyana approach it.
body:
In transfer pricing, the documents you prepared before the tax year closed decide most of the outcome; after that, you are arguing from memory against an authority that has the power to adjust, penalise and wait for the other country to offer relief.

Recall

Q. What does a 400,000 dollar transfer pricing adjustment cost when the other country gives no matching relief?

A. Tax on the same income in both countries: a lost deduction in one and tax already paid in the other, plus interest and possibly a penalty.

Q. In a tax treaty, what is the difference between the credit method and the exemption method?

A. Under the credit method, the residence country taxes foreign income but credits the foreign tax paid. Under the exemption method, it does not tax that income at all. Which applies depends on the treaty and domestic law; verify against the primary source.

Q. What is a site-specific safety plan?

A. A written plan for one site that identifies its particular hazards, the controls, responsibilities, emergency procedures and how subcontractors will comply.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I teach this as the life cycle of a dispute, because you will meet it as one. Nothing here states any country's law, any penalty rate or any time limit; verify each against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: tax adviser with transfer pricing experience in each country.

Stage one: documentation

Most countries with transfer pricing rules expect, or require, a written record of how each related-party price was set. Typically it covers the parties and their relationship, the transaction and its terms, a functional analysis, the method chosen and why others were rejected, the comparables, and the result. Some countries require it to exist by the filing deadline, which is what contemporaneous documentation means in this context. Others require it only on request, within a short period.

Why it matters so much: in many systems, having reasonable documentation in place on time is what protects you from a penalty even if the authority later disagrees with your price. Without it, an adjustment can carry a penalty on top of the tax. So the documentation is not paperwork about the price; it is insurance against the penalty.

Stage two: the adjustment

If the authority concludes a price was outside the arm's-length range, it adjusts the taxable income of the company in its country, usually toward a point in the range it considers appropriate. Some systems also make a secondary adjustment: they treat the excess amount that left the country as if it were a dividend or a loan to the foreign affiliate, which can trigger withholding tax or deemed interest on top of the primary adjustment. Ask your adviser whether a secondary adjustment exists and whether it can be avoided by repatriating the excess.

Time limits for reassessing related-party transactions are often longer than for ordinary items. A fee you charged years ago may still be open. Verify the period against the primary source.

Say that out loud now.

Stage three: relief from double tax

When one country increases your income, the other may reduce it by the same amount, called a corresponding adjustment. It is not automatic. Where both countries have a tax treaty, it usually contains a mutual agreement procedure: a process in which the two tax authorities negotiate to eliminate double tax. These processes are slow, can take years, and often do not guarantee a result. Some taxpayers instead seek an advance pricing arrangement, an agreement with one or both authorities in advance on the method for future years. It costs time and fees, and is usually worth it only for large, recurring transactions.

Stage four: after the adjustment

An adjustment for one year is rarely about one year. Once an authority decides a fee was above the range, it will usually test the same fee in every open year, and expect future years to follow the adjusted price. So the decision after an adjustment is strategic, not just a matter of paying or appealing. Do you change the agreement and the price going forward, which may be cheaper than defending every year? Do you object or appeal, knowing that any formal step has its own deadline and that missing it can end your rights? Do you seek relief in the other country at once, before its own time limits run? Each of these is a decision for your advisers in both countries together, made within days of the adjustment, recorded in the tax file with the reasons. Then update the documentation so that next year's file answers the authority's objection before it is raised.

Worked example: the life cycle in numbers

Hypothetical rates, taken from no country: 30 percent in the project's country, 25 percent in the parent's country, and a penalty of 10 percent of the adjustment where documentation was missing.

A project company paid its parent a 1,200,000 dollar fee. The project-country authority adjusts it to 800,000 dollars. Primary adjustment: 400,000 dollars of extra income, tax 120,000 dollars. With documentation in place, no penalty. Without it, 40,000 dollars of penalty. A secondary adjustment treating the 400,000 dollars as a dividend, with hypothetical 15 percent withholding, adds 60,000 dollars.

Totals in the project's country: 120,000 dollars with documentation and no secondary adjustment; 220,000 dollars without documentation and with a secondary adjustment. If the parent's country grants a corresponding adjustment, it refunds up to 100,000 dollars of the parent's tax on the 400,000 dollars, often years later. If it does not, that 100,000 dollars stays paid. The spread between the best and worst path is 320,000 dollars on one fee, and the biggest lever in it was documentation written before the year closed.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source before relying on any point.

Canada. Canada has a well-developed transfer pricing regime, based on the arm's-length principle and influenced by the OECD guidance, with an expectation of contemporaneous documentation, penalties where reasonable efforts to set and document arm's-length prices were not made, and access to mutual agreement and advance pricing processes. The details, thresholds, deadlines and penalty rules must be taken from the current legislation and the tax authority's published guidance [unverified — confirm independently].

Guyana. Guyana's approach to related-party pricing should be confirmed directly. My understanding is that Guyana has general provisions allowing the authority to adjust non-arm's-length dealings, and that more specific transfer pricing rules and documentation expectations have been developed in recent years, but the scope, documentation requirements and penalties must be confirmed with a Guyanese tax adviser against current law [unverified — confirm independently]. Whether a tax treaty between Canada and Guyana is in force, and whether it contains a mutual agreement procedure covering transfer pricing, must also be confirmed against the treaty text [unverified — confirm independently].

The practical consequence is the same in both: prepare documentation to the standard of the more demanding country, and confirm before you need it whether any route to relief from double tax actually exists between the two.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming double tax will always be relieved. It may not be, and when it is, it may take years. The control is to price conservatively within the range, document before the books close, and confirm in advance what relief route exists between your two countries.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner writes the transfer pricing documentation after the audit letter arrives. By then it is evidence of an argument, not of a decision, and it no longer protects against the penalty.

Callback

In Week 57, Elias and Devika taught what treaties do: allocate taxing rights, reduce withholding and, through tie-breakers, decide residence. The mutual agreement procedure is the part of a treaty that matters most when a transfer pricing adjustment arrives, and it is worth reading before you ever need it.

Recap

Transfer pricing is enforced through documentation, adjustments, secondary adjustments and penalties, with relief from double tax available only through corresponding adjustments, mutual agreement or advance arrangements. Documentation written in time is the cheapest protection.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: pricing a shared-service charge and an intercompany guarantee fee, step by step.
checklist: Every related-party price has documentation written before the filing deadline.
The documentation covers parties, terms, functional analysis, method, comparables and result.
I know whether each country makes secondary adjustments.
I know how long related-party transactions stay open to reassessment in each country.
I have confirmed whether a tax treaty with a mutual agreement procedure exists between my countries.
I document to the standard of the more demanding country.
I have considered whether an advance pricing arrangement is worth its cost.
A transfer pricing adviser in each country has reviewed the file.
head: Field checklist
speak: Transfer pricing is enforced in stages. First, documentation: a written record of how each related-party price was set, covering the parties, the functions, the method, the comparables and the result. In many systems, having it in place on time is what protects against a penalty even if the price is later adjusted. Second, the adjustment: the authority moves the price into the range, and some countries add a secondary adjustment, treating the excess as a dividend. Third, relief: the other country may make a corresponding adjustment, often only through a slow mutual agreement procedure under a treaty, and not always. In my hypothetical, the difference between the best and worst path on one fee was 320,000 dollars, and the biggest lever was documentation written before the year closed. Canada and Guyana must each be confirmed against current law, including whether relief exists between them.
terms: Contemporaneous documentation — transfer pricing records prepared at or before the time the tax return is filed, not after an audit begins.
Secondary adjustment — an extra adjustment treating the excess of a non-arm's-length price as a dividend, loan or other payment, often attracting withholding.
Mutual agreement procedure — a treaty process in which two tax authorities negotiate to eliminate double taxation, including after a transfer pricing adjustment.

hostile.q: Your transfer pricing report is dated after our audit letter. Why should we not apply a penalty?
hostile.a: I accept that this report was finalised after your letter, and I will not pretend otherwise. What existed before the filing deadline was the signed intercompany agreement, the board minutes and the adviser's benchmarking note on which the fee was set; here they are, with their dates. The later report expands that analysis but does not change the method or the range. I ask that you assess the reasonableness of our efforts on the documents that existed on time.

title: Pricing a Shared-Service Charge and a Guarantee Fee, Step by Step
summary: Two intercompany prices a developer sets every year: a cost-plus charge for head-office services and a fee for the parent's guarantee of a project loan. Both are worked step by step with units and hypothetical round numbers, ending in the documents that support them.
body:
An intercompany price is defensible when you can rebuild it on one page from costs, an allocation key, a comparable and a benefit, and every number on that page has a source you can hand to an auditor.

Recall

Q. What is a corresponding adjustment?

A. A reduction of income by one country to match an increase made by the other country after a transfer pricing adjustment, which relieves double tax. It is not automatic.

Q. Why does a 60,000 dollar annual related-party fee matter at exit?

A. Because it lowers net operating income, and at a cap rate it lowers value many times over, so a buyer will strip out any part above a market rate and refuse to pay for it.

Q. In a ratio test of thin capitalisation, how do you find the maximum loan from a fixed amount of sponsor money?

A. Set loan L no greater than the ratio times equity, where equity is total sponsor money minus L, and solve for L.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Day 1 gave you the principle and Day 4 the enforcement. Today we produce two prices you will actually set. All figures and rates are hypothetical, chosen for arithmetic. The methods are widely used conceptual approaches; how a particular country applies them must be verified against the primary source.

Calculation one: a shared-service charge, cost plus

Step 1, identify the costs. The parent's head office has two staff who spend part of their time on project companies, plus systems. Salary and benefits for the two staff: 240,000 dollars a year. Accounting software and office cost attributable to them: 40,000 dollars. Total cost pool: 280,000 dollars.

Step 2, remove what is not a service. The two staff estimate that 25 percent of their time is spent on the parent's own matters: its own accounts, investor relations for the parent, and board work that monitors the subsidiaries as an owner. That is stewardship, a cost of owning, not a service to the subsidiaries. Remove 25 percent: 280,000 times 0.75 equals 210,000 dollars of chargeable cost.

Step 3, choose an allocation key. Time records show hours on each project company over the year: Project A 1,200 hours, Project B 600 hours, Project C 200 hours. Total 2,000 hours. Shares: A 60 percent, B 30 percent, C 10 percent.

Step 4, allocate cost. A: 210,000 times 0.60 equals 126,000 dollars. B: 210,000 times 0.30 equals 63,000 dollars. C: 210,000 times 0.10 equals 21,000 dollars. Check: 126,000 plus 63,000 plus 21,000 equals 210,000 dollars.

Step 5, apply the mark-up. Suppose a benchmarking study shows independent providers of comparable routine administrative services earn mark-ups on cost of between 4 and 8 percent, with a middle of 6 percent. Charge 6 percent. A: 126,000 times 1.06 equals 133,560 dollars. B: 63,000 times 1.06 equals 66,780 dollars. C: 21,000 times 1.06 equals 22,260 dollars. Total charge: 222,600 dollars.

Step 6, test against reality. Would Project C, a small project, pay an outside firm 22,260 dollars a year for this work? If an outside bookkeeper and coordinator would cost it about the same, the charge holds. If C could buy it locally for much less, your allocation or your cost pool needs another look.

Say that out loud now.

Calculation two: a guarantee fee

The parent guarantees a 15,000,000 dollar construction loan to Project A. Should Project A pay the parent a fee, and how much?

Step 1, measure the benefit. The bank's quoted rate without the parent's guarantee: 8.0 percent. With it: 7.0 percent. The guarantee saves 1.0 percentage point. On an average drawn balance of 9,000,000 dollars over construction, the annual interest saving is 9,000,000 times 0.01, which is 90,000 dollars a year.

Step 2, remove passive association. Part of that saving may come simply from Project A being part of a well-regarded group, which lenders recognise even without a guarantee. That benefit is not a service the parent provides and is generally not chargeable. Suppose evidence suggests the bank would have offered 7.6 percent to Project A without a guarantee, just because of its group. The guarantee itself then saves only 0.6 percentage points: 9,000,000 times 0.006 equals 54,000 dollars a year.

Step 3, split the benefit. An unrelated guarantor would want paying for its risk, and Project A would pay only if it kept some of the saving. A common conceptual approach is to set the fee somewhere within the saving, supported by evidence of what guarantors or credit insurers charge for similar risk. Suppose the evidence supports a fee of 0.4 percent of the guaranteed drawn balance. Fee: 9,000,000 times 0.004 equals 36,000 dollars a year. Project A keeps 54,000 minus 36,000, which is 18,000 dollars a year of benefit. Both parties gain, which is what an arm's-length deal looks like.

Step 4, check the lender. Many construction lenders will not allow guarantee fees to be paid to the sponsor during construction, or will subordinate them. If the fee must accrue, the agreement must say so, and the transfer pricing file must say why accrual does not change the price.

Calculation three: the shareholder loan rate, built up

Week 60 used a rate on a shareholder loan without showing where it came from. Here is one common conceptual approach, a build-up, again with hypothetical figures. Step 1, the base rate: a published reference rate for the loan's currency and term, say 4.0 percent. Step 2, the borrower's credit spread: what an unrelated senior lender charges a project company of this risk, taken from the senior bank's own term sheet, say 2.5 percentage points, giving 6.5 percent. Step 3, the subordination premium: the shareholder loan ranks behind the bank, so an unrelated junior lender would want more. Evidence from mezzanine quotes might support 2.0 to 4.0 points; take 3.0, giving 9.5 percent. Step 4, the cross-check: does 9.5 percent sit inside the range of rates actually charged on comparable subordinated loans? If yes, document the four steps and their sources. Then go back to the sizing sheet, because a higher rate shrinks the loan an earnings-based interest cap will allow.

The page that supports each price

For the shared-service charge: payroll records, the stewardship estimate and its basis, time records, the benchmarking study, and the services agreement signed before the year began. For the guarantee fee: the bank's written quotes with and without the guarantee, the evidence on passive association, the guarantee fee comparables, the guarantee itself and the fee agreement. For the shareholder loan rate: the published source of the base rate on the funding date, the senior term sheet, the mezzanine quotes and the loan agreement. Each page is dated, and each is filed before the year's books close.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser with transfer pricing experience in each country; a benchmarking specialist for the mark-up and guarantee fee ranges.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is charging the whole cost pool and the whole interest saving. Stewardship and passive association are the two deductions auditors look for first. The control is to remove both explicitly, in writing, before applying any mark-up or fee.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner allocates head-office cost equally across projects because it is simple. An equal split of unequal effort overcharges the small projects and undercharges the large ones, and both are adjustments waiting to happen.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy and Nadia taught earned value and cost-to-complete: tie every number to a measured quantity, not a percentage guess. The shared-service charge is the same discipline. Hours recorded, costs measured, an allocation key you can show; not a percentage that felt about right.

Recap

A cost-plus charge removes stewardship, allocates by a measured key and adds a benchmarked mark-up. A guarantee fee measures the interest saving, removes passive association and splits the remaining benefit, within evidence of market fees. Each price rests on a dated page of sources.

Next: Cole on The Room: the tax auditor's meeting about your intercompany charges.
checklist: I have a measured cost pool for every shared-service charge.
I remove stewardship costs before charging anything.
I allocate by a measured key such as recorded hours.
My mark-up comes from a dated benchmarking study.
For each guarantee, I have bank quotes with and without it.
I remove the benefit of passive association before setting a guarantee fee.
My guarantee fee leaves the borrower with part of the saving.
Every price has a dated support page filed before the books close.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two prices I set every year. First, a shared-service charge, cost plus. My hypothetical head office cost 280,000 dollars. I remove a quarter for stewardship, the parent watching its own investments, leaving 210,000. I allocate that by recorded hours, 60, 30 and 10 percent across three projects, and add a benchmarked six percent mark-up, so the charges are about 133,600, 66,800 and 22,300 dollars. Second, a guarantee fee. The bank quotes 8 percent without my parent's guarantee and 7 with it. But part of that saving comes just from being in my group, which is not chargeable, so the guarantee itself saves 0.6 points, about 54,000 dollars a year on the average balance. A fee of 36,000 dollars, inside market evidence, leaves the project 18,000 of benefit, so both sides gain. Every number sits on a dated page I can hand an auditor.
terms: Cost plus — a pricing method that charges the supplier's costs plus a mark-up earned by comparable independent suppliers.
Stewardship — a parent's activity in monitoring its own investment in a subsidiary, which is a cost of owning rather than a chargeable service.
Passive association — the benefit a subsidiary gets simply from belonging to a group, such as better loan terms, which is generally not a chargeable service.

hostile.q: Your parent charges Project A for a guarantee. Wouldn't the bank have given Project A a good rate anyway, just because it belongs to your group?
hostile.a: Partly, yes, and we took that out. The bank quoted 8.0 percent with no support and 7.0 percent with the guarantee, and our evidence suggested about 7.6 percent for Project A purely because of the group. We priced only the remaining 0.6 points of benefit, and set the fee below that saving and within market guarantee fees, so Project A keeps part of the benefit. Here are the quotes, the analysis and the agreement.

title: The Tax Auditor Asks About Your Intercompany Fees
summary: A scene in which a tax auditor in the project's country opens a review of the fees your project company pays its parent. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state, with a monthly thread on ethics and anti-corruption.
body:
When a tax auditor asks about your intercompany fees, the meeting is decided by the file you built months ago; your job in the room is to hand it over cleanly, answer only what is asked, and never improve the story.

Recall

Q. Why do you remove stewardship before setting a shared-service charge?

A. Because a parent monitoring its own investment is a cost of owning, not a service to the subsidiary, and charging for it is a common reason for adjustment.

Q. What does a secondary adjustment do?

A. It treats the excess of a non-arm's-length price as a dividend, loan or other payment, which can trigger withholding or deemed interest on top of the primary adjustment.

Q. Why should a developer prequalify contractors on safety, not only on price?

A. Because a contractor's safety record predicts incidents, delays and liability on your site, and in some enforcement systems the owner or controlling contractor can share responsibility for hazards. Screen safety before the lowest price is chosen.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sit in this room. An auditor is entitled to examine your intercompany dealings, and the professional response is neither defensive nor chatty. I play the auditor's role on our bench, so I will tell you what the auditor is actually doing.

The scene

This is a hypothetical scene. An auditor from the project country's tax authority has written asking for the project company's intercompany agreements and transfer pricing documentation for the last three years. The meeting is in the auditor's office. With you are your local tax adviser and the project company's finance manager. The project company paid its parent a development management fee, a shared-service charge and a guarantee fee.

The auditor opens: "Thank you for coming. We have the documents you sent. I would like to understand who actually did the development management work, because we see a local team in the project company payroll."

The lines to say

"The local team handles site coordination and day-to-day consultant administration. The parent's team handled approvals, design management, procurement strategy and lender reporting. The functional analysis on page 4 of the file lists each function and who performed it, and the timesheets for the parent's staff are in appendix C."

If asked about overlap: "We considered that when the fee was set. The local team's cost is not included in the parent's fee, and the comparables in the benchmark were selected for scopes that exclude site coordination. If you see an overlap we missed, please show us and we will look at it seriously."

If asked something you cannot answer: "I want to give you an accurate answer rather than a quick one. Our adviser will confirm that in writing by Friday."

Say that out loud now.

Later the auditor turns to the guarantee fee: "The bank lent to the project company. Why should the project company pay its parent for a guarantee?" The line to say: "Because the bank quoted a higher rate without it. We have the two written quotes, we removed the part of the saving that came simply from being in the group, and the fee leaves the project company with part of the remaining benefit. That analysis is on page 9." Then stop, and let the auditor read page 9.

The lines never to say

Never say "everyone in the industry charges this." It is a claim without evidence and it invites the auditor to test the industry.

Never say "the fee doesn't matter, it's all within the same group." It tells the auditor you think the arm's-length principle does not apply to you.

Never volunteer a new justification that is not in the file, such as "it also covered our brand." If it is not in the documentation, it was not part of the pricing decision, and adding it in the room looks like the story is being rebuilt.

Never suggest, however lightly, that the matter could be "resolved" informally. Even a joke about it can be read as an offer of something improper.

The question behind the question

The auditor's question about the local team is really: is the project company paying twice for the same work, and is the parent being paid for work it did not do? Every follow-up will circle that. Once you see it, you know what evidence matters: who did what, recorded at the time, and how the fee was set to exclude duplication.

Behind the auditor's later questions is another: is this a taxpayer who sets prices honestly and documents them, or one who reverse-engineers them? Your conduct in the room answers that as much as the file does.

When to stay silent

When the auditor is reading a document, stay silent. When the auditor states a provisional view you disagree with, let them finish, then ask one question: "Could you tell us which part of the analysis leads you there?" That turns a conclusion into a point you can address. Do not argue every point in the meeting. Your adviser can respond in writing, with evidence, which is both calmer and more persuasive.

How to hold your state

Auditors are not adversaries in the personal sense; they are professionals checking a file. Treat the meeting as a review of evidence, not a judgment of your character. Slow your speech, keep answers to two or three sentences, and let your adviser answer technical tax points. If you feel the urge to defend yourself, that is the signal to stop and point to a page. Breathing drills belong in the car park, parked, before you walk in, not during the meeting; check with your doctor if you have any condition that might be affected.

After the meeting

Within a day, send a short written note to the auditor, copied to your adviser: what was asked, what was provided, and what will follow and by when. Then keep every commitment in it. An auditor who receives what was promised, on the day it was promised, reads the next answer more generously.

Monthly thread: ethics and anti-corruption

Mr Shabazz, rooms with officials who can cost you money are where integrity is most tested. Anti-bribery laws in many countries, including laws with reach beyond their own borders, forbid offering anything of value to influence an official, and some forbid even small facilitation payments; verify the laws that reach you against the primary source. A gift, a meal, a favour to a relative, a "consulting fee" to someone close to the official: each can be a bribe in substance, whatever it is called.

Set your rule before you need it. You offer nothing of value to any official, you record every interaction with authorities, you refuse any request for an informal payment and report it to your lawyer, and you would rather pay a fair adjustment than buy a favourable one. That rule protects you legally, and it protects the one asset that cannot be rebuilt quickly: a reputation lenders and partners trust.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in this room is improvising: adding justifications that are not in the file, or arguing to win the moment. The control is preparation: read your own file the day before, know where each answer sits, and let the documents speak.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the audit as a negotiation and tries to win every point in the room. The outcome is decided by evidence, and evidence is best delivered in writing.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught working with professionals: what privilege covers, and that your adviser's role must be clear. In an audit meeting, your adviser speaks to technical tax; you speak to facts you know first-hand. Knowing which is which keeps both of you credible.

Recap

The auditor wants to know who really did the work and whether you set prices honestly. Answer from the file, never add new reasons in the room, ask which part of the analysis drives a provisional view, confirm in writing, and offer nothing of value to any official.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: transfer pricing, with a Red Pen drill on an intercompany services agreement.
checklist: I read the whole transfer pricing file the day before an audit meeting.
I know which page answers each likely question.
I answer facts I know first-hand and let my adviser answer technical tax.
I never add a justification that is not in the file.
I ask which part of the analysis drives a provisional view.
I confirm every commitment in writing within a day and keep it.
I offer nothing of value to any official, ever.
I report any request for an informal payment to my lawyer.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a tax auditor asks about my intercompany fees, the meeting is decided by the file I built months earlier. The auditor's real question is usually whether the project company is paying twice for the same work, or paying the parent for work it never did. So I answer from the file: who did what, recorded at the time, and how the fee was set to exclude overlap. I never say everyone charges this, never say the fee doesn't matter because it's all one group, and never add a reason that is not in the documents, because that looks like the story is being rebuilt. If the auditor states a view I disagree with, I let them finish and ask which part of the analysis leads there, then respond in writing. I confirm commitments within a day. And I offer nothing of value to any official, ever.
terms: Tax audit — a review by a tax authority of a taxpayer's returns and records to test whether tax was correctly reported.
Provisional view — an auditor's preliminary conclusion, open to response before any adjustment is made.
Facilitation payment — a small payment to an official to speed up a routine action, prohibited by some anti-bribery laws; verify the law that applies.

hostile.q: Your project company employs a local team. Why did it also pay the parent a development management fee?
hostile.a: Because the two did different work. The local team handled site coordination and consultant administration; the parent's staff handled approvals, design management, procurement strategy and lender reporting. Page 4 of the file sets out each function and who performed it, the parent's timesheets are in appendix C, and the benchmark was built on scopes that exclude site coordination. If you see overlap we missed, show us and we will address it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 61 Review: Transfer Pricing
summary: Six questions on the arm's-length principle, methods, documentation and guarantee fees, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a defective intercompany services agreement, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: every price between your own companies must be the price strangers would agree, proved by a record of who did what and what strangers charge, written before the year closes.

Recall

Q. In the auditor's meeting, what should you never add in the room?

A. A justification that is not already in the file, because it looks like the story is being rebuilt.

Q. What is the binding limit when sizing a shareholder loan?

A. The smallest of the loan amounts produced by the ratio test, the earnings test and the bank's distribution test, after checking the rate is arm's length.

Q. What does a contingency structure in a cost plan separate?

A. Design contingency, construction contingency and owner's contingency, each held by a different party for a different kind of unknown.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, transfer pricing is the place where a cross-border structure most often meets a tax authority. If you can answer these six questions aloud, you can brief an adviser, review a draft policy and sit in an audit meeting without losing the thread. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. State the arm's-length principle in one sentence.

Answer: Prices between related parties should be the prices unrelated parties would agree in comparable circumstances.

Question 2. What two things does an arm's-length analysis look at?

Answer: First, what was actually done: the functions each party performed, the assets it used and the risks it carried. Second, what unrelated parties charged in comparable transactions.

Question 3. Which pricing methods do most of a developer's work, and for what?

Answer: A direct comparable price for loans and guarantees, cost plus a benchmarked mark-up for shared services, and comparison with independent managers' fees for development management.

Question 4. What was the root cause in the GlaxoSmithKline case, and what is Rule 61?

Answer: A price separated from the bundle it paid for. Rule 61: never set an intercompany price without a written analysis, made at the time, of the whole bundle the payment buys, tested against comparables that buy the same bundle.

Question 5. Why does contemporaneous documentation matter even if the price is later adjusted?

Answer: Because in many systems reasonable documentation in place on time is what protects against a penalty, even when the authority disagrees with the price. Written after the audit letter, it no longer does.

Question 6. In a guarantee fee, what is passive association and why is it removed?

Answer: The benefit a subsidiary gets simply from belonging to a group, such as a better loan rate without any guarantee. It is not a service the parent provides, so it is removed before pricing the guarantee.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Cole set out the arm's-length principle, functional analysis, comparables and the main methods. Ford and Cole took the GlaxoSmithKline case, decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012, and drew Rule 61 on pricing the whole bundle. Sage priced what intercompany fees do to cost, value, outside investors and tax. Elias walked the life cycle of a challenge, from documentation to relief, and compared Canada and Guyana in principle. Nadia built a cost-plus charge, a guarantee fee and a shareholder loan rate. Cole ran the auditor's meeting and the month's thread on anti-corruption.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical intercompany services agreement summary and find the defects before reading on.

Services Agreement, Parent to ProjectCo. Services: general support and oversight as required. Fee: 8 percent of ProjectCo's total development cost, payable monthly in advance. Allocation: Parent's head-office costs shared equally among all project companies. Mark-up: 15 percent, consistent with group practice. Term: effective from the start of the project; signed at year end. Benchmark: to be prepared if requested by any tax authority. Approved: Parent board.

The defects. First, "general support and oversight" does not define the services, and "oversight" is stewardship, which is not a chargeable service. Second, 8 percent of total development cost charges a percentage on land, finance costs and the fee itself, not on the work managed, and has no comparable behind it. Third, payable monthly in advance means ProjectCo pays before any service is received. Fourth, an equal allocation ignores how much effort each project actually takes. Fifth, a 15 percent mark-up justified by "group practice" is justified by nothing: the comparable is the market, not the group. Sixth, signed at year end but effective from the start, without saying it confirms an earlier arrangement, invites the backdating question from Week 60. Seventh, a benchmark "to be prepared if requested" is documentation written after the audit letter, which loses penalty protection. Eighth, only the parent approved it; ProjectCo, the payer, did not. Ninth, it charges both a percentage fee and an allocation of the same head-office costs, which risks paying twice for the same work.

The corrected version defines each service, excludes stewardship, prices development management against independent fees, allocates shared costs by recorded hours, applies a benchmarked mark-up, is signed before services begin by both boards, and attaches the benchmark on the day it is signed.

Kema's method for any Red Pen: read the document three times with three questions. First, what exactly is being bought, and could a stranger tell from the page? Second, how is the price built, and does every number have a source outside the group? Third, who approved it, when, and does the date on the page match the day it was signed? Most defects in an intercompany document fall under one of those three. If you train yourself to ask them every time, you will find the defects before an auditor does, which is the entire point of the drill.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a joint venture partner who asks, "Why is your company charging our project fees, and how do I know they are fair?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Our parent does real work for the project: approvals, design management, procurement and lender reporting, and it guarantees the construction loan. It charges for that work at the price an unrelated firm would charge, which tax authorities in both countries require anyway. Each fee has a written agreement signed before the work, a record of who did what, and a benchmark against independent firms. We remove anything that is just us watching our own investment, and anything the project gets simply from being in our group. You will see every fee listed in the pro forma, and two returns: the project's return after all our fees, and our return including them. If any fee sits above the market range, we will bring it down."

Score your own answer. Did you lead with the bottom line? Did you name the arm's-length principle in plain words? Did you mention documentation before the work, and removing stewardship? Did you offer the two-return view? Under two minutes?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is pricing intercompany charges by what you want each company to earn. The control is a pricing policy and benchmark set before the year, and Rule 61 applied to every bundle.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking transfer pricing is a problem only for large multinationals. Any developer with companies in two countries that pay each other has transfer pricing, whether or not he has a policy.

Callback

In Week 58, Devika and Elias taught the routes cash takes home: dividend, interest, fee and return of capital. Fees are the route this week examined most closely, and the lesson is that the fee route is only as strong as the evidence behind each price.

Recap

Arm's length means the price strangers would agree. Analyse functions, find comparables, choose the method, document before the year closes, price the whole bundle, and expect relief from double tax to be slow and uncertain.

head: The six questions
speak: Transfer pricing means that every price between my own companies, a development fee, shared costs, a loan or a guarantee, must be the price strangers would agree. The analysis asks what each company actually did, what assets it used and what risks it carried, and what unrelated parties charged for comparable work. For a developer, the main tools are direct comparable prices for loans and guarantees, cost plus a benchmarked mark-up for shared services, and comparison with independent development managers. I remove stewardship, which is the parent watching its own investment, and passive association, the benefit of just being in the group. I price the whole bundle, as the GlaxoSmithKline case showed, and I document everything before the year closes, because that is what protects against penalties. Relief from double tax exists but is slow and never guaranteed.
terms: Arm's-length price — the price unrelated parties would agree for the same transaction in comparable circumstances.
Benchmarking study — a documented search for comparable transactions or companies used to set an arm's-length range.
Advance pricing arrangement — an agreement in advance with one or more tax authorities on the transfer pricing method for future years.

hostile.q: Your services agreement says the fee is 'consistent with group practice'. Where is the market evidence?
hostile.a: Group practice is not evidence, and our current agreement no longer relies on it. Here is the benchmarking study we commissioned before the year began, the functional analysis showing which parent staff performed which services, the hours-based allocation and the agreement signed by both boards before services started. The mark-up sits inside the benchmarked range.
